question: What happens to aircraft in a holding stack as the lowest aircraft leaves to start its approach?

options.text: They all leave the stack together
The others are cleared down one level at a time
They hold at the same level until each one is cleared to approach separately
They climb to make room for new arrivals

explanation: Aircraft are stacked with vertical separation; as the bottom aircraft leaves to fly the approach, those above are descended (shuttled) one at a time.

question: Why must pilots follow the published holding procedures accurately?

options.text: Deviations risk taking the aircraft outside the protected holding area
Because the timing is used to measure fuel flow
Because accurate holding is needed to keep the autopilot engaged
Because ATC uses the pattern timing to calculate the expected approach time of the next aircraft

explanation: Deviation from the in-flight procedures for holding incurs the risk of excursions beyond the perimeter of the protected holding area.

question: A standard holding pattern uses:

options.text: Turns in either direction at the pilot's choice
Right-hand turns above FL140 and left-hand turns below it
Right-hand turns
Left-hand turns

explanation: The standard holding pattern has right turns; left-hand patterns are annotated on the chart and are mirror images.

question: Turns in a holding pattern are made at:

options.text: Rate 1 only, whatever bank that requires
30° bank or rate 1, whichever requires more bank
20° bank or rate 1, whichever requires the greater bank angle
25° bank or rate 1 (3°/s), whichever requires less bank

explanation: All turns in the holding pattern are at a bank of 25° or a rate of 3° per second, whichever requires the lesser bank.

question: How should a pilot allow for a known wind in the holding pattern?

options.text: Correct only the inbound heading
Apply corrections to heading and timing
Correct only the outbound timing and not the headings flown
Apply no correction; the pattern is flown as headings

explanation: Procedures depict tracks; pilots maintain them by applying corrections to both heading and timing during entry and while holding.

question: When does outbound timing in a holding pattern begin?

options.text: Over or abeam the fix, whichever is later
Over the fix, in all cases
At the end of the inbound leg, before the turn starts
When the outbound turn is started

explanation: Outbound timing begins over or abeam the fix, whichever occurs later; if abeam cannot be determined, timing starts on completion of the turn to outbound.

question: What is the length of the outbound leg in a holding pattern at FL150?

options.text: 1 minute
1 minute 15 seconds
1½ minutes
2 minutes

explanation: The outbound leg is 1 minute at or below 14 000 ft and 1½ minutes above 14 000 ft.

question: What is the length of the outbound leg in a holding pattern at 9000 ft?

options.text: 45 seconds
2 minutes
1½ minutes
1 minute

explanation: At or below 14 000 ft the outbound leg is 1 minute.

question: If the outbound leg of a hold is defined by a DME distance, when does it end?

options.text: When the aircraft is abeam the fix
After 1½ minutes or at the DME distance, whichever is later
As soon as the limiting DME distance is reached
After 1 minute, whatever the DME reading

explanation: A DME-defined outbound leg terminates as soon as the limiting DME distance is attained.

question: A pilot cannot comply with the normal holding procedures. What must be done?

options.text: Climb to the next level and continue holding there
Inform ATC as soon as possible
Fly a larger pattern without telling ATC
Leave the hold and divert

explanation: If for any reason a pilot cannot conform to the procedures for normal conditions, ATC should be informed as soon as possible.

question: In normal conditions, the maximum holding speed up to and including 14 000 ft is:

options.text: 230 kt
265 kt
240 kt
210 kt

explanation: Up to 14 000 ft: 230 kt (170 kt where the holding is limited to Category A and B). Above 14 000 to 20 000 ft: 240 kt; above 20 000 to 34 000 ft: 265 kt; above 34 000 ft: Mach 0.83.

question: A hold is limited to Category A and B aircraft. What is the maximum holding speed up to 14 000 ft?

options.text: 200 kt
140 kt
230 kt
170 kt

explanation: For holdings limited to Category A and B aircraft only, the speed is 170 kt.

question: In normal conditions, the maximum holding speed above 14 000 ft up to 20 000 ft is:

options.text: 280 kt
230 kt
265 kt
240 kt

explanation: Above 14 000 ft up to 20 000 ft inclusive the speed is 240 kt.

question: In normal conditions, the maximum holding speed above 20 000 ft up to 34 000 ft is:

options.text: 265 kt
Mach 0.83
280 kt
240 kt

explanation: Above 20 000 ft up to 34 000 ft inclusive the speed is 265 kt.

question: The maximum holding speed above 34 000 ft is:

options.text: 265 kt
280 kt or Mach 0.80, whichever is less
Mach 0.83
Mach 0.80

explanation: Above 34 000 ft the holding speed is Mach 0.83, in normal and turbulent conditions.

question: In turbulence, an aircraft may hold at up to 280 kt (or Mach 0.8, whichever is less) below 34 000 ft:

options.text: Only below 14 000 ft
Only after clearance from ATC, unless publications show the area allows it
Only in holds limited to Category A and B aircraft
At the pilot's discretion, without telling ATC, provided the pattern is flown in the normal time

explanation: The turbulence speed of 280 kt (Mach 0.8) is used only after prior clearance from ATC, unless publications indicate the holding area can accommodate it.

question: The initial segment of an approach is published for a speed above 230 kt. What should the associated holding speed be?

options.text: 170 kt for all aircraft
Mach 0.83 at all levels
Also promulgated at the higher speed, wherever possible
Still limited to 230 kt, the speed for all holdings at or below 14 000 ft

explanation: When the hold is followed by an initial segment promulgated at a speed higher than 230 kt, the holding should also be promulgated at that higher speed wherever possible.

question: How many entry sectors are defined for joining a holding pattern, and what flexibility applies at their boundaries?

options.text: Three, with no flexibility
Three, with ±5° flexibility either side of each boundary
Two, with ±15° flexibility at the inbound track
Four, with ±10° flexibility either side of each sector boundary

explanation: There are three entry sectors based on the aircraft's heading approaching the fix, with a 5° flexibility zone either side of each boundary.

question: In a parallel (sector 1) entry to a standard right-hand hold, after reaching the fix the aircraft:

options.text: Turns right onto the outbound heading, then right again to the fix
Turns right to follow the holding pattern immediately
Flies outbound 30° from the reciprocal on the holding side
Flies outbound parallel to the inbound track on the non-holding side, then turns left back

explanation: Parallel entry: turn onto an outbound heading parallel to (reciprocal of) the inbound track for the appropriate time, then turn left to return to the fix (or intercept inbound), then follow the hold.

question: In an offset (sector 2) entry, after reaching the fix the aircraft flies a track at what angle from the reciprocal of the inbound track, on the holding side?
explanation: Offset (teardrop) entry: fly a track 30° from the reciprocal of the inbound track on the holding side for the appropriate time, then turn right onto the inbound track.

question: In a direct (sector 3) entry, after reaching the fix the aircraft:

options.text: Turns right and follows the holding pattern
Continues straight ahead for 1 minute before turning right
Turns left to fly parallel to the inbound track
Flies outbound 30° off the reciprocal

explanation: Direct entry: on reaching the fix, turn right and follow the holding pattern.

question: On a parallel or offset entry, how long is the outbound leg flown?

options.text: For 30 seconds, then the turn back to the fix is begun
For 2 minutes in all cases
For the holding leg time appropriate to the altitude
Until reaching the MSA

explanation: The outbound heading is held for the appropriate period of time for the altitude (1 minute up to 14 000 ft, 1½ minutes above).

question: A holding clearance from ATC will specify:

options.text: Only the expected approach time
Only the holding level
The holding fix and the speed to fly, with no level
The fix, pattern (unless published), level and EAT or onward clearance time

explanation: The clearance gives the location of the hold, pattern details unless routinely published, the holding level, and EAT or onward clearance time.

question: Before reaching the holding fix, the pilot should ensure that the aircraft is level at the holding level at least:

options.text: 10 NM before the fix
5 NM before the fix
2 NM before the fix
1 minute before the fix

explanation: The aircraft should be level at the holding level at least 5 NM before the holding fix.

question: In ATC terms, a "shuttle" is:

options.text: A transfer from one holding pattern to another
A level change en route between reporting points
An approach flown immediately after leaving the hold, without a procedure turn
A climbing or descending manoeuvre in a holding pattern

explanation: A shuttle is a climbing or descending manoeuvre in a holding pattern, e.g. "shuttle in the hold to FL40".

question: From where is an aircraft normally cleared to leave the hold to start the approach?

options.text: From the fix, although radar may vector it from any point in the pattern
Only after a second complete circuit of the hold
From any point the pilot chooses
Only from the end of the outbound leg, after the pilot has requested to leave the hold

explanation: It is usual to leave the hold at the fix, but where radar is used the controller may vector the aircraft from any position in the pattern.

question: ATC clears an aircraft to leave the hold at a specific time for a timed approach. What should the pilot do?

options.text: Leave at the end of the current outbound leg
Adjust the pattern so as to leave over the fix as close as possible to that time
Hold until told again by ATC, as the time is only an estimate and may be revised
Leave immediately and slow down on the approach

explanation: The pilot should adjust the leg lengths to depart from overhead the holding fix as close as possible to the stated time.

question: What minimum obstacle clearance is provided throughout the holding area?

options.text: 150 m, up to 300 m in mountainous terrain
600 m everywhere
300 m (984 ft), up to 600 m in mountainous terrain
300 m in the holding pattern, reduced to 150 m in the entry areas

explanation: The designer applies an MOC of 300 m (or up to 600 m in mountainous terrain) throughout the holding area, including the entry areas.

question: Outside the holding area there is a buffer area. What are its width and obstacle clearance?

options.text: 5 NM wide, with full MOC throughout its width
5 NM wide, with MOC reducing from full value to zero at its edge
2 NM wide, with full MOC throughout
10 NM wide, with half the holding area MOC applied throughout its width

explanation: A buffer area 5 NM wide surrounds the holding area, with MOC decreasing from full at the holding area boundary to zero at the outer edge.
